Yes. 

The central turn in the story occurs when Ilse's estranged or distant son, Jonas, unexpectedly calls her on a Tuesday morning, and she chooses not to answer, instead locking the vibrating phone away in the cash register. 

This is **surprising** because an earlier conversation with a passenger established that Ilse hasn't heard from Jonas and doesn't know if he is coming for Christmas. When he calls at a completely unusual time (Tuesday morning during work hours, rather than a casual Sunday afternoon), it creates immediate tension and the expectation that she will answer to find out what is wrong or if he is visiting. Her refusal to pick up—and actively hiding the phone—subverts this expectation.

At the same time, her reaction is deeply **appropriate** to her established character and the themes of the story. Throughout the narrative, Ilse is depicted as a woman of stoic silence who values predictable, physical routines (pulling the ferry rope just as Henning did) and appreciates people who don't talk much. She feels alienated from Jonas's modern, fast-paced life ("offices with glass," "sentences in meetings she didn't understand"). Locking the phone away to return to the ferry rope—which "wanted nothing from her except hands"—fits seamlessly with her quiet, self-protective nature and her reliance on routine to cope with emotional distance and loss.
